items.title: 12.1.3 Meaning of the Phrase "x approaches a"

blocks.text: Symbolically it is written as "\(x \to a\)" which means that \(x\) is sufficiently close to \(a\) but different from the number \(a\), from both the left and right sides of \(a\) that is \(x - a\) becomes smaller and smaller as we please but \(x - a \ne 0\).

blocks.title: Point to remember
blocks.text:
The symbol \(x \to 0\) is quite different from \(x = 0\).
\(x \to 0\) means that \(x\) is very close to zero but not actually zero.
\(x = 0\) means that \(x\) is actually zero.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
"Smaller and smaller" here is about the size of \(x - a\), i.e. the distance \(|x - a|\) between \(x\) and \(a\) on the number line. From the left \(x - a\) is negative (e.g. \(1.99 - 2 = -0.01\)), from the right it is positive, but in both cases its size shrinks towards \(0\).
So \(x \to a\) means: \(0 < |x - a|\) and \(|x - a|\) can be made as small as we please. The "\(0 <\)" part is the condition \(x \ne a\).

blocks.caption: Our table (not in the book): values of x approaching a = 2 from both sides; the distance shrinks but is never 0.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why must \(x\) stay different from \(a\)? Because the limit describes what a function does near \(a\), not at \(a\). Many important functions have no value at \(a\) itself.
Example: \(f(x) = \frac{x^{2} - 4}{x - 2}\) has no value at \(x = 2\) (it gives \(\frac{0}{0}\)). But for every \(x \ne 2\) it equals \(x + 2\), so as \(x \to 2\) the values approach \(4\). The phrase "\(x \to 2\)" lets us talk about this without ever putting \(x = 2\).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: When asked the meaning of \(x \to a\), state three things: (1) \(x\) comes as close to \(a\) as we please, (2) from both the left and the right of \(a\), (3) \(x \ne a\), i.e. \(x - a \ne 0\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(x \to a\): \(x\) gets as close to \(a\) as we please, from both sides of \(a\).
2. \(x\) never equals \(a\): \(x - a \ne 0\).
3. \(x \to 0\) (very close to \(0\), not \(0\)) is different from \(x = 0\) (exactly \(0\)).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Approaching from one side only. \(x \to 2\) means values like \(1.99\) and \(2.01\) both; one side alone gives a one-sided limit (12.3.1).
2. Writing \(x \to a\) and then putting \(x = a\) in an expression that becomes \(\frac{0}{0}\). Near \(a\) we may simplify (cancel \(x - a\), since \(x - a \ne 0\)); at \(a\) we may not divide by \(0\).
